utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. May we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning, counsel, good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. Mark Harmon, April Carter, Bronagh McKenna, Barney Thomas, Rafael La Cruz and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the participants in the proceedings. General Perisic is represented as in yesterday, Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith, Chad Mair, Tina Drolec, Deirdre Montgomery and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the court. I will address the third prong of Perisic's 7(1) responsibility, specifically the provision of men from the VJ Special Unit Corps to participate in the Pancir operation to take Mount Zuc. The Defence has argued in paragraph 814 of its final trial brief that no unlawful acts have been alleged in conjunction with the Pancir operation to take Mount Zuc, and more specifically, that there's no nexus between the Mount Zuc operation and the scheduled incidents. It's the Prosecution submission that the Defence fundamentally misunderstands the crimes of which Mr. Perisic is charged. The indictment lays out in paragraphs 40 through 46 that the underlying crime base is a protracted campaign of shelling and sniping upon Sarajevo resulting in the killing and wounding of thousands of citizens. One must look at the scheduled incidents as representative of this campaign. I'd like to first turn to the campaign itself. The campaign against Sarajevo began in May of 1992. By 30th of 1992, Slobodan Milosevic had already declared the bombardment of Sarajevo to be bloody and criminal, for which there was no justification. 30th Personnel Centre members Ratko Mladic, Stanislav Galic, Dragomir Milosevic and, for a brief period, Cedo Sladoje, orchestrated and executed this campaign. Martin Bell described the siege. He indicated: "It was a little bit as if the Great War was being refought in a modern urban environment. No one was spared from VRS sniper artillery. This was Russian roulette on a grand scale." In his final trial brief even Perisic himself does not dispute that civilians were targeted in Sarajevo. This can be found in the Defence final trial brief at paragraph 554. The first scheduled victims were a mother and their child who were struck by a VRS sniper bullet while walking down the street on September 3rd, 1993. This is scheduled incident B-1. Following Perisic's promotion to the Chief of General Staff in August of 1993, fire intensified over the winter. If we can now briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the speaker to slow down or provide the text to the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard that, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please slow down, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm doing my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During the winter of 1993, two sniping and three shelling indents occurred during these months. The first, a man working to clear rubbish was shot on 2 November, 1993, and that's scheduled incident B-2. A woman was shot while riding her bicycle on 6 January, 1994, scheduled incident B-3. Six children were playing when a VRS shell fell upon them, killing all six and injuring three more. Eight more people were killed and 18 were injured when shells fell on a Dobrinja residential area on 4 February, 1994. Finally the Markale market was struck on 5 February, killing 60 and injuring over 140 more; scheduled incident A-3. As will be described further, the Pancir operation to take Mount Zuc in which Perisic deployed VJ Special Unit Corps members also took place between December 1993 and February 1994. However, even during non-peak periods, civilians were not safe. Scheduled incidents B-4, B-5 and B-6 took place in the summer of 1994 where three adults and a child were sniped in a tram on 19 June, 1994. Two teenage girls were shot while walking down the street on 26 June, 1994. And a 13-year-old boy window shopping was struck by a sniper's bullet on 26 June, 1994. If we can please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Bascarsija market --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, now you may proceed, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Bascarsija market was shelled during this peak, killing two and injuring seven on 22 December, 1994. Afeza Karacic and Sabina Sabanic were sniped on a tram on 23rd November, 1994. The Court may remember in Mr. Harmon's opening remarks that Ms. Karacic still bears the wounds that she suffered on that fateful day. A woman was shot gathering firewood in her own backyard on 1 December, 1994 and three more people were sniped on a tram on 27 February, 1995. If we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Two more people were sniped on a tram on 3 March of 1995. This spring also saw the introduction of air-bombs against Sarajevo, although even the Defence expert Djokic acknowledged it to be totally inappropriate and wrong to use air-bombs in an urban environment. Nonetheless, two air-bombs were launched on 24 May, 1995 alone, killing two and injuring seven in scheduled incidents A-5 and A-6. In response to this firing and aggression, the UN Rapid Response Forces were deployed in June of 1995. This month was particularly dangerous due to VRS firing 150 artillery and mortar rounds per day as described by witness Per Anton Brennskag. This included the firing on the water distribution centre, killing seven and injuring 12 on 1 July, 1995. The summer culminated with the killing of 35 persons and the injury of 78 more at the Markale market on 28 August, 1995. The VRS continued this campaign against Sarajevo until 21 November, 1995. The scheduled incidents give detail to 405 of the thousands of victims subject to this siege. Perisic served as VJ Chief of General Staff for 26 months of this siege. Turning now to the Mount Zuc operation that occurred in the context of the siege. The Mount Zuc operation and Perisic's assistance to it detailed at paragraphs 483 to 502 in the Prosecution's final trial brief. Perisic met with Slobodan Milosevic, Ratko Mladic, Radovan Karadzic, and Momcilo Krajisnik and others on 13 December of 1993. At that meeting, Karadzic identified the strategic objectives of the Bosnian Serbs, one of which was to partition Sarajevo. Karadzic emphasised that Sarajevo is a priority and a key to the war. He went on to say that, "In Sarajevo we have to capture some elevation points that will ensure our drive." Finally, he indicated that Zuc is especially important. On 14 December, 1993, Perisic and Mladic met twice. In the first meeting, Perisic committed weapons. In the second meeting, he committed to providing about 100 professionals by 20 December, 1993, all to the disposal of the SRK and equipped for combat. On 14 December, 1993, Mladic also issued a supplement to his Directive 6, which stated that in addition to SRK, VJ Special Forces up to 120 men would carry on an attack along the Vogosca, Zuc and Popovici axes. The VJ Special Forces were men from the 72nd Special Brigade, the Guards Brigade, the 63rd Parachute Brigade and the Armoured Brigade. Each of these brigades formed parts of the VJ Special Unit Corps that were directly subordinated to Mr. Perisic. Readiness for the attack was to take place on 19 December. However, prior to that on the 15th, Perisic directly met with members of the 72nd Special Brigade and ordered them to deploy and to take part in the VRS offensive operation against Zuc. When the men from the 72nd Brigade arrived, 30th Personnel Centre member Galic briefed them on the upcoming actions. He told them if Zuc was taken, all of Sarajevo would be under SRK control. A similar sentiment was given by Perisic when he spoke with the men of the 72nd, where he indicated that Zuc was a strategic location and needed to be controlled by Bosnian Serb forces. If we can now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's part of slowing down, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In excess of the numbers described in the supplement to Directive 6, by 31 December 1993 approximately 200 members of the guards Brigade alone had deployed to the front line. While there, the Guards Brigade engaged in offensive and defensive combat operations and trained snipers. On 7 January, 1994, the UN Security Council president condemned the actions in Sarajevo, particularly condemning the continuing military pressure and relentless bombardment by the Bosnian Serb forces. This can be found at Exhibit P2475. As described in the annexes to the Commission of Experts' report, admitted as P1535 at page 36, from 4 to 7 January alone, Sarajevo was struck by 3.915 shells. As an aside, the Defence claims in paragraph 520 of its final trial brief, that the Prosecution has not stated the purpose for the commission of experts' report. The Trial Chamber admitted both P112 -- 1112, the Commission of Experts' report as it was published in instalments in the newspaper Borba, and P1535, the annexes to the report without restriction in its decision of 21 December, 2009 relating to MFI documents. P1536, the report in its official form was limited to notice at transcript page 7382, lines 2 through 6. Moving back to the facts of the Zuc campaign. The day after the condemnation by the UN Security Council president, Perisic arrived in Vogosca and met with VJ and VRS commanders, as well as RS politicians. 30th Personnel Centre members Mladic and Galic were present along with the head of the VJ Special Unit Corps. These corps, the men part of the corps would not pull out until 27 to 30 January, 1994. As seen by placing the Mount Zuc campaign into context, these actions by General Perisic did assist in the continued bombardment of Sarajevo for which he is charged. I will wait for questions from the Chamber or I'll turn it over to Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Morning, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I just need to change the volume on this. Yesterday evening and yesterday, I reflected on the proceedings, I read the transcripts of the proceedings yesterday. And before I make my submissions on 7(3), there are two points from the transcript that I need to address and would like to address. The first deals with an answer that I gave Your Honour, Judge Moloto, which is found at 14661, where the question and where my answer was: "The position we assert here is identical to the situation in your hypothetical situation." A few lines later, I said, "I'm saying that the situation is identical in terms of the framework of our case." Now, the facts of the hypothetical were not identical and are not identical. What is is the applicable legal principles are the same in this case, and aiding and abetting does not differentiate, Your Honours, whether the substantial assistance to crimes is provided to armed forces or whether they are national or international. So my statement in respect of being identical dealt with the legal framework with which to apply the law as to any given factual situation. Now, Your Honours, the other point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you move to the next point then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just remind you that, one, that was not a hypothetical case; it's a practical case. Secondly, that, in fact, it was given as an analogy. The underlying question that I put to you has not been answered and I don't know whether you to intend to answer it. My question to you was, what is your authority for the proposition that a commander is guilty of aiding and abetting the crimes of his subordinate, merely for the fact that he gave them arms and ammunition, paid their salaries, send them to war and while they were at war, committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can also I'm asking for authority from the Tribunal's jurisprudence and case law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't have case law at my fingertips. What I do have is the law that says that aiding and abetting -- first of all, there is no case like this case in the Tribunal, okay. This case is unique on its facts and this case will make case law. So I can't give you authority, Your Honours, to your question, Your Honour. There is authority --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, that was the question I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much, Your Honour. Now, the second point that we started out yesterday's proceedings, Your Honour, with a question that you posed on cumulative charging, 7(1) and 7(3), the question was not answered, I know, to your satisfaction. So I have asked Ms. McKenna to make a submission on this point, then I'll -- after she makes that submission, I will then proceed, Your Honours, with 7(3) submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As Mr. Harmon said, I'm going to make just a very brief submission on the issue of cumulative charging to provide a little more detail on the Prosecution's position on this issue. In the Prosecution's submission, liability under Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) are not mutually exclusive. The Blaskic appeals judgement at paragraph 91 provides that the provisions of Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) connote distinct categories of criminal responsibility, and so, where both categories or where both modes are charged in the same case, each mode of liability reflects a different aspect of an accused's alleged criminality. So with specific reference to this case, Your Honour, aiding and abetting is a form of accessory liability, and it requires a principal perpetrator who carries out the crime. The OTP's submits that Perisic is liable for aiding and abetting the principal perpetrators of the crime, but that Perisic himself is not the principal perpetrator. Rather his liability rests on his aid or his provision of positive acts of assistance to the crime. And under Article 7(3), Perisic is charged with liability for his failure to prevent or punish the acts of his subordinates and this legal characterisation would be best if the Trial Chamber feels that Perisic's criminal conduct is better categorised as a failure to act in respect of his subordinates, when he was under a duty to do so. So on the facts of the present case, the Prosecution submits that the Perisic's is liable under both Article 7(1) and Article 7(3), however, as you recognised yesterday, the case law of the Tribunal accepts that it's illogical to find an accused liable for both -- for failing to prevent and punish the very acts that he aided and abetted, and therefore the Trial Chambers usually decide where they find that the that both convictions could be entered, they enter the one that is more direct, that is, Article 7(1). Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just note that you probably moved slightly away from the question I put. You are talking about cumulative charges in the same case. I asked cumulative charges that are mutually exclusive for the same conduct. But you may sit down. I just want you to remember that that was my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The first point I would like to address, Your Honour, is the issue of whether the regulations on the applicability of international laws of war on the armed forces was applicable to General Perisic. You will recall that the regulations were discussed by Mr. Starcevic. There's a discussion on the regulations in our pre-trial -- our final brief at paragraph 717 to 720. The exhibit is P2304. Now, a violation of those regulations could constitute a violation of military discipline of which Perisic was required to enforce. The Defence position on the applicability of the regulations is found in the Defence brief, paragraphs 975 to 979, the Defence asserts that the regulations did not impose a obligation on General Perisic because, one, Mr. Starcevic testified that those provisions applied only in cases of armed conflicts of an international nature. And, two, during the period of the indictment, there was no international armed conflict. Our position is those regulations did apply to General Perisic and they did impose obligations on him. We say that because Mr. Starcevic, shortly after he explained to Your Honours that the provisions applied only in a conflict of an international nature, went on to say that because the offences were so grievous and so terrible, the parties in the SFRY in the conflict signed a special memorandum committing themselves to apply all the rules that would otherwise be applicable only in an international armed conflict. You can find Mr. Starcevic's testimony at page 6976 through 6977. Now, on the basis of those regulations, the VJ General Staff issued two orders requiring adherence to the provisions of International Humanitarian Law. Now, there was a transition between the SFRY and the FRY. The P198, which is a newspaper report relating to the declaration of the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia constitution, on that date the FRY issued a declaration in which they said, and I quote: "The FRY shall adhere strictly to all obligations which the FRY undertook in the past on the international stage." Moreover, Your Honour, P1183, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Law on Defence, Article 19, states: "Members of the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia taking part in armed combat shall, under all circumstances, adhere to the rules of international laws of war and other rules ..." And it carries on. So our submission is, Your Honour, that the regulations on the applicability of the international laws of war in armed conflict situations did in fact impose an obligation on General Perisic. Those obligations continued after the SFRY became the FRY. Now I'd like to turn to 7(3), Your Honours. In respect of 7(3), there are three elements to the offence. The first is, there must be is superior-subordinate relationship established. The second, the superior knew or had reason to know that his subordinate was about to commit or had committed the underlying crime. And three, the superior failed to take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent the subordinate from committing the crime or punish the subordinate for having done so. I'm not going to address the second and third elements. We have addressed the knowledge element of 7(3) extensively in our brief, and that's found at paragraphs 563 to 683. The Defence concedes that Mr. -- General Perisic failed to punish his subordinates. You can find that in the Defence pre-trial brief paragraph 135, subpart (v), and they take the position that he did not have effective control and therefore he could not have prevented his subordinates from having committed crimes. What I want to take focus on is that the issue of superior-subordinate relationship, and the existence of a superior-subordinate relationship. Now, the test of a whether a superior-subordinate relationship exists is whether there is effective control, which means whether there is a material ability of the superior to prevent or punish the subordinate from having perpetrated offences. It's a fact-based determination. It is not -- it is a fact-based determination. Your Honours have to take a look at the evidence in this particular case, and the parties have defined for the court in their briefs, what are the indicators of effective control. You can find in our brief at paragraph 697, and in the Defence brief, paragraph 75. But those indicators that we cite are not the only indicators. There are a range of possibilities, and they include: The position held by the superior, the capacity to issue orders, the nature of the orders which the superior had capacity to issue, whether his orders were actually followed, the power to take disciplinary action, the authority to promote officers, and the authority to remove officers. Our position is, Your Honour, that personnel centre members serving in the -- VJ personnel serving in the personnel centre members were VJ officers, and as such Perisic had effective control over them. The Defence position, which is found at paragraph 207 of its brief, is that the VJ officers serving in the VRS and the SVK were members of those armies and not of the VJ. So that's where we part company. I'd like to take a look at the evidence, Your Honour, that supports our position. First of all, let me take a look at the evidence that shows there was de jure authority over personnel serving in the personnel centres. First, Perisic was, of course, the highest ranking officer in the VJ. He was superior to all other officers. Two, the personnel centre formations, if we could have -- the personnel centre formations, as you can see on the screen before you, were part of the VJ General Staff. They were under the sector on manning, mobilisation and systematic issues under the personnel administration. So they were part of the VJ General Staff. Three, Mr. Starcevic testified that persons who were assigned to the 30th and 40th Personnel Centre were VJ members according to the law. You can find that testimony at page 5489, lines 12 to 15. And as a matter of law, Perisic had authority over VJ personnel. Now, in addition, Your Honour, there were -- there was considerable litigation in the FRY relating to the status of persons serving in the personnel centres. The first litigation I'd like to refer to -- by the way, you can find that discussion in our brief at paragraphs 789 to 792. The first case I'd like to discuss with Your Honours was the case of Colonel Blagojevic. Colonel Blagojevic was somebody this Tribunal is familiar with. He was convicted for his participation in crimes in Srebrenica. But prior to coming to The Hague, he sought compensation for unused annual leave. His request for compensation was denied by the 30th Personnel Centre. And he appealed. He appealed claiming that he took part in armed operations in Bosnia on the basis of orders he received from his superior and that he was a member of the VJ. The Supreme Military Court agreed with Mr. Blagojevic. They stated in the judgement that's in front of Your Honours: "It is not contentious that Blagojevic was outside the VJ during the period for which he is seeking compensation, i.e., as a VJ member, he was part of the former -- he was in a part of the former SFRY territory on the orders of a superior officer, and he did not take his annual leave" for the years that are indicated. So the court in the Blagojevic case held that he was a professional VJ soldier, VJ law applied to his request for compensation, and they granted his request. The second case involves Dragomir Milosevic, who as you know, was convicted in this Tribunal for crimes committed in Sarajevo. General Milosevic brought a charge, brought a claim, I should say, for compensation for wounds that he received in combat in Sarajevo. The FRY challenged his claim. They asserted that he was performing duties on behalf of the VRS, and as part of its military. The court rejected the FRY's position. The court said, and on the monitor before you: "It was established beyond a reasonable doubt that the plaintiff was a professional soldier of the VJ at the time of his wounding, and was on its payroll at that time." There's another judgement I won't go into in detail, Your Honours can find it, it's Prosecution Exhibit 872. It holds essentially the same thing. It is a claim by Dragomir Milosevic for family separation allowance. Now, the judgements of the Supreme Military Court were followed in decisions by the 30th Personnel Centre. So when a claimant subsequently went before a -- the administrative body to make a claim, he was granted compensation. If we could take a look at the claim in the decision, the administrative decision by General Mladic for unused annual leave, that is Prosecution Exhibit 1919. And you will see that in -- on the monitor in front of you, that there's a finding that General Mladic was serving in Military Post 3001, which we know is the military post for the 30th Personnel Centre. And they go on to say that: "In accordance with the position of the Supreme Military Court in Belgrade, that the law was violated, given that it is undisputable that the above-mentioned did not receive the fixed salaries for the duration of the period in question and was serving, that is, working in the Yugoslav Army, the above-mentioned is entitled to a salary pursuant to the cited provisions of the law." So it is our submission, Your Honour, that as a matter of law, persons serving in VJ personnel centres were VJ members, but that doesn't conclude the inquiry that's required of Your Honours in assessing whether or not General Perisic had effective control over members of the personnel centres. It's only some evidence that he had effective control. You have to look, Your Honour, at other factors which we, both parties, have identified as factors indicative of effective control. I would like to go through some of those with you. The first is that the salaries and benefits for persons in the personnel centres were paid by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They were not paid by the Republika Srpska. They were not paid by the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Those entities paid salaries and benefits to their soldiers, not to VJ soldiers. Another indicator of effective control is whether or not General Perisic had the capacity to promote his subordinates serving in the personnel centres. The Defence argues, in its Defence brief paragraphs 414 et seq, that promotions in the VRS were made final in the VRS, and the only steps taken in the VJ were to verify those promotions to protect the status rights of an officer. Now, we certainly accept part of that proposition. There were promotions within the VRS and the SVK. However, the process of verification as its referred to, was not merely to protect status rights. The process of verification was a determination of whether or not the person who was serving in the VRS or the SVK merited a promotion in the VJ. In other words, promotions were discretionary; they were not automatic. Now, there are two types of promotions that occurred in the VJ. There were regular promotions and there were extraordinary or exceptional promotions. It depended -- Perisic's authority depended on the rank of the person to be promoted. In respect of the rank of generals, the president of the FRY had the authority to make a promotion. General Perisic had the authority to make a promotion of his subordinates serving in the personnel centres, up to and including the rank of colonel. I'd like to focus on the promotions to the rank of general. Normally the procedure would be that the SDC would be advised by General Perisic whether the person who was seeking -- for whom a promotion was sought merited the promotion. The SDC was not a rubber stamp. They needed guidance and advice from General Perisic. They turned to him to make recommendations on the merits of the officer to be promoted. If we can go to the next visual aid which is Prosecution Exhibit 709, which is a text from the 14th session of the SDC in October of 1993 where General Perisic said in relation to the promotion of VJ officers in the 30th and 40th Personnel Centre: "The standard there is how the men have demonstrated themselves in combat and in the specific work they do." You can find that, as I say, at Prosecution Exhibit 709, page 39. Now, at that same session, Slobodan Milosevic said the following: "If we are going to resolve this matter, I think we should resolve it in conformity with a proposal by General Perisic, instead of being an instrument of transmitting the proposals they have given, whereas we are not familiar with the criteria. I think that General Perisic should ask General Mladic for an opinion about all this and come up with his own views and then present us with proposals to address the issues individually." Now, this required General Perisic to make a qualitative analysis on the persons from the personnel centres for whom promotions of an equivalent rank were sought in the VJ. General Perisic exercised that discretion and that authority. He recommended for some generals and he recommended against the promotions of other generals in the VJ. If we can turn to Prosecution Exhibit 786, which is a text from the session of the 37th session of the SDC on June 7th, 1995. Perisic reported to the SDC that the SVK was seeking promotions of two persons, Celeketic and Loncar, to the ranks lieutenant-general and major-general respectively. General Perisic advised the SDC as follows: "Given that they are guilty for the situation over there, the General Staff has assumed a stance that these should not be verified." And the SDC adopted General Perisic's recommendation. Now, at the same session, he proposed 12 generals and he made recommendations positively for promotions for six and proposed that the SDC reject the remaining six. And you can see that in the text that is before you, that is Prosecution Exhibit 786, page 32. And you can see some familiar characters from this Tribunal. You can see that he positively recommends the promotion to the rank of general to General Gvero, General Miletic, General Tolimir, but he rejects six others including Dragomir Milosevic, "who is a commander of the Sarajevo Corps and who was also an SDS member." So he rejects six, I won't name them all. Those recommendations as well were accepted by the SDC. Now, if we turn to the issue of exceptional promotions, because there was two types of promotions, as I say, there were regular promotions and exceptional promotions. In respect of the exceptional promotions, the same qualification applied. The FRY president could make those exceptional promotions for persons up to the rank of general. The rank of general, I should say, and General Perisic could make exceptional promotions for persons up to the rank of, and including, the rank of colonel. The president could make those recommendations at the proposal -- exceptional promotions at the proposal of General Perisic. Now, you'll find the description of the law in P197. It's Article 46. The exceptional promotion, what did it mean? It meant that there was going to be special recognition for exceptional contributions of officers in the line of their duty. I refer Your Honours to the transcript 5498. Now, Perisic, General Perisic did exercise his authority to exceptionally promote members of the VRS and the SVK and he did so frequently. We will take a look first at P1731, if we can. Now this, Your Honours, 1731 is a -- from the personnel file of Vinko Pandurevic, who we are familiar with in this institution. Vinko Pandurevic was promoted three times, exceptionally, by General Perisic. The first two entries you can see were before Srebrenica. The third exceptional promotion to infantry colonel was on the 31st of December, 1995. This was months after General Perisic had been informed by Slobodan Milosevic that thousands of people had been killed in Srebrenica. And after he had ample opportunity to inquire as to the events in Srebrenica. If we could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 1897 which is another example. This is a file from -- personnel file of Dragan Obrenovic, who we are familiar with in this institution, who has been convicted of crimes committed in Srebrenica. Both he and Vinko Pandurevic were members of the Drina Corps, the corps that was responsible for the atrocities in Srebrenica. We can see in Mr. Obrenovic's personnel file, three exceptional promotions given by General Perisic, the third after the events in Srebrenica. Now, as I say, he also made exceptional promotions for people in the SVK. So if we could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 2866. This is an individual by the name of Veljko Bosanac. He was a member of the 40th Personnel Centre and we can see that this is an order that was issued by General Perisic to exceptionally promote Mr. Bosanac. So he turned to a different promotion and a different -- of a different individual which is also an indicator of effective control, and that is the promotion -- the extraordinary promotion or exceptional promotion of General Mladic, which occurred in the VJ. If we could have that on the screen, please. This is the exceptional promotion of General Mladic that occurred on the 16th of June, 1994. It was pursuant to an order of President Lilic and you can see in the text, you'll see underneath the exceptional promotion, if you go down a little bit lower, directly underneath that, Your Honour, you'll see it says, "Ratko Mladic, son of Nedzo, Commander of the Main Staff of the 30th Personnel Centre." You can see that this exceptional promotion -- as I say exceptional promotions were made on the recommendation of General Perisic pursuant to Article 46. This exceptional promotion, Your Honour, came into effect on the 16th of June, 1994. It came into effect two weeks before General Mladic received an equivalent promotion in the SVK. So if we could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 1903.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not sure I'm with you. You say it came into effect two weeks before General Mladic received an equivalent promotion in the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't mean the SVK, I misspoke. Thank you. The VRS. Okay. So two weeks before General Mladic received the promotion to the rank of colonel-general in the VRS, he had been promoted in the VJ. That promotion, Your Honour, of General Mladic had nothing to do with the process of verification. It had nothing to do with the protection of status rights. It was a straight promotion in the VJ. In our -- I think we can conclude, or it's our submission, Your Honour, in respect of promotions that General Perisic was in fact a critical figure in the promotion process of members of the VJ. He advised on promotions, he made promotions, and it's clear that those promotions were not promotions that were rubber stamped. Now, let me turn to a different element, another indicator of effective control. That's the issue of whether Perisic had the authority to issue orders and issue commands. We had a discussion, a very illuminating discussion, I should add, by Mr. Starcevic who told us the distinction between orders and commands in the VJ. He described what I will say is an order, or a "naredba", which he described as an order defining the duties, rights and responsibilities of individuals. He gave an example of transfer orders as a naredba. He described a command, "naredjenje," as an operational command and, as such, a part of the chain of command. You can find his testimony, Your Honour, at 5462 to 5463. Now, I'd like to focus first of all on transfer orders, naredba. General Perisic could issue transfer orders personally. Otherwise they were issued by the personnel administration, the branch to which he had delegated that authority. What we have seen from the evidence is that General Perisic and the personnel administration transferred people to and from the VJ to the 30th Personnel Centre, to the 40th Personnel Centre, sometimes between the 30th and the 40th Personnel Centre, sometimes to the Ministry of Defence. People in the VJ were fungible. They could be -- they were required to follow orders, they were transferred wherever the needs of service required. In fact, when you look at some of these personnel files, the career trajectory looks like a pinball bouncing back and forth between the different units within the personnel centres. Now, these orders to transfer back and forth were obeyed. That's another indicator of effective control. They were obeyed both by SVK personnel and -- I am sorry, by 30th Personnel Centre members and 40th Personnel Centre members. Now, we know that some of those orders were not obeyed. We also know, Your Honours, that that was a disciplinary offence. Insubordination. But we also know that it was not in the public interest of the FRY to proceed against people who had been insubordinate for refusing to transfer from the VJ to a different country. So what did the VJ do? The VJ found other ways to get rid of people who were insubordinate. I believe, I don't have it in the top of my head, I believe it's in the 14th session of the SDC where General Perisic says, if people won't go, we'll find another way to get rid of them. But let me show you, Your Honours, some of the orders that were transfer orders that were issued personally by General Perisic. If we could go to Prosecution Exhibit 1524, please. Now, this, Your Honour, is an order issued by General Perisic. It was issued on the 5th of October, 1994 for an individual by the name of Bogdan Sladojevic. Mr. Sladojevic was being transferred on General Perisic's order from the 40th Personnel Centre to the 1st Army of the VJ. If we could go to Prosecution Exhibit 1893. Your Honour, I don't have a visual on 1893, but let me direct your attention to 1893. This is a personnel file and in the personnel file you'll see that General Perisic transfers General Krstic, who we know from this Tribunal, from the 30th Personnel Centre to the VJ school. If we go to 16 -- Prosecution Exhibit 1690, this is a personnel file for an individual named Smiljanic. Mr. Smiljanic, as you'll see at the bottom of the personnel file for Mr. Smiljanic, he was deployed in accordance with the needs of the service to the Federal Ministry of Defence, this is on General Perisic's order. Finally, if we go to Prosecution Exhibit 1522, we'll see the personnel file once again of Bogdan Sladojevic. And in this situation, you'll see that Mr. Sladojevic, who had been at the VJ school in Belgrade was ordered by General Perisic to go to the 30th Personnel Centre. Now, there's more -- naredba didn't only apply to transfer orders. If we could have Prosecution Exhibit 1777, that is doc ID 601-0672. This, Your Honour, is a 16 September 1995, it is a command issued by General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A naredjenje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. I'm going to get there, Your Honour. This is a command issued by General Mrksic, a naredjenje based on a naredba that he received from General Perisic. And you'll see that, Your Honour, in the top highlighted portion with the objective of carrying out the order of the chief of the VJ General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, and if you go to the parallel text in B/C/S, you'll see that's a naredba. And in that order that is issued to General Mrksic who was the commander of the SVK, he asked certain things be done, that General Novakovic do certain things. And then he says in subpart (3): "Give a briefing on the dismantling upon reporting to the General Staff of the VJ in Belgrade." This is an order -- this is the naredba that was ordered by General Perisic to General Mrksic is being complied with in the command that he issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying that what Mr. Mrksic is giving here is a naredjenje, and not a naredba.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am saying that, Your Honour. That's correct, he receives an order from General Perisic, issues a command to enforce General Perisic's order. So you can see, as you'll see on the left in upper case letters it says "order". To the right, it says naredjenje. That's the command that General Mrksic is giving to his subordinates to execute General Perisic's order. If you have any questions on that, Your Honour, I'm happy to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said to the right, it says naredjenje, I'm trying to look for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It says "naredjenjum," Your Honour. I'm sorry. You see the top two yellow highlights? In between there's a word that says order, that's not highlighted. That is the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to turn to commands, because General Perisic had the authority to command and issue commands to persons who were in the personnel centres. And those -- he did so and those commands were obeyed. If we could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 2412. Now, this, Your Honour, is a report from Slobodan Peric, who at the time he issued this document was the commander of the 18th Corps of the SVK, and he sends this document to General Perisic. So it is addressed to the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ. And it's a report about the performance of officers who were serving in the SVK. And what he says, what he -- Mr. Colonel Peric says is "based on your oral" and it says "order," but if you go over to the B/C/S version of it, it's "based on your oral naredjendje" or "command". So with this document, Your Honour, you can see that there was a command issued orally by General Perisic to Colonel Peric who was a commander of the SVK 18th Corps and Colonel Peric is obeying it. If we can turn to Prosecution Exhibit 1925. Now, this, Your Honour, is a document from General Perisic. It is a command. It is dated the 24th of March, 1995, and it is a command to form a co-ordinating staff for assistance to the 40th Personnel Centre. Now, just direct Your Honours, you'll see where it says order for the formation of a co-ordinating staff for the assistance. If you go over to the equivalent part in B/C/S, is "naredjendje". And if you go to the word "order" in the English, it's "command," "naredjenje". In that list of people who were supposed to participate in the, this particular co-ordinating staff were two members of the 40th Personnel Centre. Mr. Starcevic was shown this document and shown the two people who were in the 40th Personnel Centre. Mr. Starcevic testified that General Perisic was properly exercising command over members of the 40th Personnel Centre when he issued this command. You can find that testimony at 6761 through 6763. This command, Your Honour, was obeyed. Now, Your Honours, let me turn to another indicator of effective control, and that is the ability of the superior to discipline and to punish his subordinates. General Perisic believed he had that capacity. If we could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 2413, please. Now, this is a document, to put it into context, Your Honour, this is a document that was issued on the 9th of November, 1995. It was a document that was issued after the debacle in the Krajina, after the defeat of the forces in the Krajina. And this is a document that was issued by General Perisic and it says: "With the aim of establishing responsibility and solving the status of service for professional soldiers of the Yugoslav Army who served in the 40th Personnel Centre," and then he gives an order. And his order is, if you go down to subpart (2) of this order: "For officers for whom reasonable suspicion that they had committed a violation of discipline or a crime has been established, disciplinary investigation will be initiated through authorised officers, and it will be completed latest by 20 November, 1995." Now, I note, Your Honour, in the context of this order which applies to VJ members who served in personnel centres, this is many many many months after rockets with cluster warheads fell on the city centre of Zagreb. General Perisic is not exercising his authority, his disciplinary authority because persons in the 40th Personnel Centre committed war crimes. He is issuing his order because he is dissatisfied with the conduct of persons who had been responsible in his view for the debacle in Croatia. Now, disciplinary proceedings in fact took place. We've heard evidence of that, Your Honour. I'll cite only one. This is discussed generally in our brief starting at paragraph 269, but I'll discuss one of those incidents. It's the situation, Your Honour, of Colonel Bulat. Colonel Bulat was an individual who was the commander of the 21st Corps of the SVK. He surrendered the 21st Corps to the enemy. General Perisic was quite upset with that, and if we go to P2204. Go to 2204. If it's not there, I am sorry, Your Honour, I did not make a visual aid for Your Honours' benefit. In P2204, General Perisic was upset with Bulat and others and what he said in respect of Bulat was: "I can dismiss him, but I will not dismiss him." So he acknowledges that he has the capacity to dismiss Bulat. Instead he says, "You will instigate a criminal report." That's found at P2204. And thereafter, Your Honours, the VJ did in fact complete, they conducted and completed an investigation against Colonel Bulat into his conduct as the 21st Corps commander. Five witnesses were called at that proceeding. The VJ investigative committee recommended that proceedings be instituted against Bulat and that he be punished. Now, you'll see a complete description, discussion in our brief in other examples in paragraphs 738 and 739. Your Honour, I can see the time and this would be -- about to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do so, was he punished?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an interesting question, it's answer is we don't know because we had the testimony of Mr. Novakovic. General Novakovic who was a Defence witness who appeared. He said to his knowledge he knew Colonel Bulat, he didn't know if he was or didn't think he had been, but let me just say, Your Honour, that it was in the interest of -- I'll be discussing that after the break. It was in the interest of the FRY not to make public these kinds of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, but they --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The answer is I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There are inquiries going on, we just want to know how far it went. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It went so far as having witnesses called and having a recommendation that it should proceed further. Thereafter, I don't know whether he was actually punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we take it up later. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We were talking before the break about General Perisic's ability to discipline and punish his subordinates. I'd like to turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to find out, is there any other person? You said you didn't know whether this particular person was punished, is there any other person that was ever punished?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm about to address four of them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to address the situation of the four SVK generals. Generals Celeketic, Novakovic, Mrksic and Bjelanovic. They were viewed by General Perisic as being responsible for the defeat of the SVK and General Perisic had a problem, however, because of their high profile. He had the authority, of course, to institute disciplinary proceedings against them, but he took a more cautious approach, he consulted with the SDC. If we turn to Prosecution Exhibit 2203, we can see the text of the collegium of the Chief of the VJ General Staff from the 6th of November, 1995, and this is General Perisic. This is his approach to the SDC, he says: "As I wrote to the Supreme Defence Council that all four of them should be prosecuted, 'Is it in your interest that they would be prosecuted?' They said yes. And 'Is it in your interest that that would not be made public?' Yes. And now if we pension them off and then prosecute them, there are different sanctions than if we do not pension them off and prosecute them. And they said as it was necessary to calm things down and not to make public, then they made a Solomonic decision to pension off all four of them and they pensioned them off." Now, we know from the evidence that the -- this collegium text is the 6th of November, 1995. We know that those four generals served in the SVK, I think until October of 1995. But based on a decision that was taken by the SDC, they were retroactively retired to the 31st of December, 1994. Now, Your Honour, we assert that that was punishment of those four generals for their conduct while they were serving as VJ members in the SVK. They were covert punishments because as the SDC said, they didn't want to make these public. There weren't tangible effects of that punishment beside the loss of prestige. These four generals were entitled to pension benefits through the full period of their active military service which was in October of 1995. They were deprived of those benefits, because the pension benefits only went up to the 31st of December, 1994. Now, Your Honours, the SDC's fears about public trials were justified. It would have exposed the truth about the personnel centres. A trial would have exposed what the personnel centres were in fact. It would have reveal the way logistics were supplied to the personnel centres. In short, Your Honours, it would have exposed the deception of the personnel centres, and I just refer Your Honours to paragraphs 753 and 754 of our brief. Your Honour, you had a question to ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I just wanted to say given just that scenario that you have painted, what did you then say was the effect of this requirement to keep things under the carpet on the material ability to punish the subordinates by the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't think it had any -- what I think, Your Honour, is they were punished period, whether it was covert or not covert. General Perisic had the authority and at the direction of the SDC he could get rid of people whether there were public trials, public disciplinary proceedings and the like. As he said in the 14th session, we'll find another way to get rid of them. In this situation, this is a covert punishment of these four generals. So while General Perisic had had fully the capacity and the authority over VJ members to institute disciplinary proceedings, the way those disciplinary measures were implemented against people were either overt in some sense or covert. So I don't think it had, you know -- I think frankly that's the way the situation was, that's the way General Perisic received his directions from the SDC and that's the way people were punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm actually thinking in particular punishment for the crimes alleged in the indictment, not only these four, but everybody that the Prosecution alleges should have been punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think General Perisic had a duty and a responsibility as a commanding officer to institute proceedings against people he knew had committed crimes. The political environment doesn't relieve him in any way of that responsibility. He had the responsibility to take measures which he failed to take. He had the capacity, he exercised the capacity. He just didn't do it in respect of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But do you -- from what you've been saying this morning, it looks like the political environment which you say is -- should not be taken into account was the very political environment that constrained him in punishing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no evidence before this Chamber that General Perisic was relieved of his responsibilities as a commander at the direction of his political superiors. He had an obligation, regardless of the political climate, to discharge his responsibilities. He could not, he could not rely on the climate, if you will, to discharge responsibilities. He could have done a number of things. He could have taken ameliorative steps when he knew there were war crimes were being committed. He could have issued orders, commands, directions, he could have brought people in, consulted with his people, he could have even resigned if there was a direction to not proceed. He did none of those. In fact, Your Honour, as I'll discuss later, he assisted war criminals avoiding justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next to the case of Mr. Antic and Mr. Vujic. Those two cases are described in our brief at paragraphs 741 to 746. Those are both members of the 30th Personnel Centre, the VRS. Both these individuals went AWOL from the VRS. Both these individuals were prosecuted in a VRS military disciplinary court and in the case of Antic and Vujic, their sentence was the loss of status as an active duty serviceman. The VRS forwarded those judgements to the VJ and asked the VJ to take further action. It was up to the VJ then, Your Honours, to decide what to do about its personnel who had committed disciplinary measures in the VRS and in these cases, Your Honour, they took different actions. In the Antic case, they considered the matter and they discharged him from the VJ. In the Vujic case, they came to a different conclusion. They kept Mr. Vujic, they didn't terminate his service. Mr. Vujic continued to serve in the VJ until 2005. So ultimately, Your Honour, the decision-maker was the VJ on the offences that had been committed in the VRS. Now, Your Honour, let me turn to the -- another issue of determinations which is another indicator of effective control. General Perisic had the authority to terminate members of the VJ who were serving in the personnels and he did so. I have described or we have described in our brief in paragraph 761 a number of such incidents, but I will like to show you Prosecution Exhibit 1904 which is a VJ order issued by General Perisic. It is in relation to Ljubisa Beara. Mr. Beara was convicted in this court of genocide. And it is dated the 6th of August, 1997. And you can see that pursuant to General Perisic's order, Mr. Beara is terminated from the VJ. Now, he also exercised that authority when it came to members of the SVK. If we could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 1684, you'll see in this case, Your Honour, this is the case of an individual by the name of Bora Poznanovic, and Mr. Poznanovic was serving in the -- he had served in the 40th Personnel Centre as the SVK 7th Corps commander. Now, he was retired from the VJ three years after the debacle in Croatia. He was retired on the 30th of June, 1998 by General Perisic. The next issue, Your Honour, another indicator of effective control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These two, I see the reasons for these two people given is that they've had 40 years of pensionable service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And that was -- that's under Article 107 of the Law on the VJ. There are a number of criteria by which you can -- someone can be terminated from service. What is interesting, frankly, about 40 years or 30 years of effective service, within that framework there was the opportunity for General Perisic to discipline people who didn't follow his orders, and he says so in one of the SDC sessions. He says, we can find another way to get rid of them. You know, we can say they've met their pensionable service years. So yes, they relied on that law, that provision of the law, but they relied on that provision of the law also to covertly sanction members of the personnel centres who had committed disciplinary infractions and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess then my question would be, these two, had they also committed some infractions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We assert in our indictment that Colonel Beara was one of the persons responsible for the massacres committed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, but what I'm saying is although the ostensible reason is 40 years pensionable service, was in fact the authentic reason the fact that they were being punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can't say that, Your Honour, I kind of doubt it myself. I think that probably the reason was was that he had completed 40 years of service. What is interesting to note about this retirement on the termination of the 30th of June -- I'm sorry, let me get the right date on Mr. Beara -- on the 6th of August, 1997, is it's two years after the crimes that were committed in Srebrenica, two years after General Perisic knew about what happened in Srebrenica and had time to investigate and inquire about what happened in Srebrenica. He could have terminated Colonel Beara much sooner than two years after the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I'd like to turn to another issue that's raised in the Defence brief. That a deals with General Djordje Djukic's evidence. General Djukic, for your information, was a member of the 30th Personnel Centre. He was on the VRS Main Staff, he was in charge of logistics. We have asserted, Your Honour, that VJ officers who were serving in the personnel centres retain their VJ identification cards. The Defence takes a contrary position. They assert in paragraph 220 of their brief that the Prosecution failed to prove that officers who were serving in the VRS were given VJ identity cards. Secondly, they assert that the VJ did not issue military identity cards to officers serving in the VRS during the conflict period. That Djukic's evidence that he possessed a VJ identity card has not been corroborated and cannot be relied on, and that this failure of proof demonstrates the existence of three separate, independent and autonomous armies. If we could have Prosecution Exhibit 1653. This -- General Djukic had two identity cards when he was arrested. He had this card which was issued in Han Pijesak. It's a VRS card. And if we could turn to the next element, this is General Djukic's VJ identity card that was issued to him on the 25th of January, 1995. And you'll see the translation of what is on the cover in Cyrillic in the lower left-hand side of this image is: "Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Yugoslav Army, military identity card." So you must judge, Your Honours, you've heard testimony from Defence witnesses who said they didn't receive a VJ identity card. I ask you to consider their evidence in light of the evidence that General Djukic had received a VJ identity card. Now, Your Honour, let's take a look, if we can, at what General Perisic has to say whether VJ personnel were serving in the VRS and the SVK. I'm going to play a portion of a film for Your Honours and it has script underneath it. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I have just a moment, Your Honour, I just want to check something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is not the film, Your Honour, that I wanted played. I will read the text of Prosecution Exhibit 2879. Unless you have it. Your Honour, let me read the text. This text, Your Honour, is found P2879, the timer number is 1:01:35 to 01:02:23. This is the clip of film, Your Honour, that is relevant. Did that come up on Your Honours' screens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have a transcript on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, this isn't very successful, Your Honour. Let me try reading the text then into the record. I have given Your Honours the citation. Let me read this to you: "Almost no decision in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, although it had its political leadership, nor in Republika Srpska, was made without an agreement of the state leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time. Analogously, the army also had close time, and there were several reasons for that. Firstly, because that was one of single army. Secondly, because it had its members in all those areas, and thirdly, because it had equipment which was getting its logistics support mostly from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." If Your Honours go to the actual film, which is P2879, there is a text that's underscored. Now, Your Honours, I want to turn to a slightly different element, but related, and that is the issue of General Perisic's material ability to punish the criminal conduct of his subordinates serving in the personnel centres. We assert that it was concurrent with the material ability of Karadzic, Martic, and commanders of the VRS and the SVK. The Defence takes a number of positions on this account. Paragraph 155 of the Defence brief, the Defence says that the Prosecutor's Office is articulating a novel theory is that both legally and factually unfounded. The principal position of the Defence, which is repeated throughout their brief, paragraphs 154, 857 and 858, is that the principle of unity of command excludes the existence of any superior position being held by someone who is outside the chain of command. And what they assert is that upon receiving their assignment on duty in the VRS, personnel centre members entered the exclusive and sole chain of command of the VRS with Karadzic as the supreme commander of VRS. As such and in accordance with the principle of unity of command, both Perisic -- Perisic, both legally and practically, could not exercise control over members of the VRS, who were regulated via the 30th Personnel Centre. It's our position, Your Honour, that the Defence confuses two concepts. The principle of unity of command, and the concept of effective control. They are separate and distinct principles. In respect of whether the position is legally unfounded, I draw Your Honours' attention to the case, the Popovic judgement, paragraph 2025 where the Court stated at follows: "It is necessary to distinguish the military concept of the singleness of command from the assessment of effective control. For the proper functioning of an army, there can only be one individual in command of any particular unit at one time. However, the test for the superior-subordinate relationship rests on the ability to effective control. There is no -- sorry, let me read that again, I misread it. However, as the test for the superior-subordinate relationship rests on the ability to effectively control - as opposed to the exercise of that control - there is no exclusivity to the determination of effective control." In the next paragraph, Your Honour, paragraph 2026, the Court goes on to say: "In addition, given the purpose of the law relating to superior responsibility, a superior cannot rely on a principle of singleness of command, described to ensure army efficiency, in order to escape responsibilities which relate to the suppression of the gravest of crimes." So it's our submission, Your Honour, that in respect of the jurisprudence of in Tribunal, it has been -- there is a legal recognition of the Prosecution's theory. Second of all, I'd like to assert, Your Honour, and I will have to go into closed session, that there in fact existed a parallel chain of command between General Perisic and the SVK. If we could go into closed session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session. You want closed, not private.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Private session is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our submission that we have established through the evidence that there was in fact a parallel chain of command between General Perisic and the SVK. The command -- the parallel chain of command went like this: In the SVK, and using General Mrksic as an example, in the SVK, the supreme commander was Martic, and the head of the SVK, the commander of the Main Staff was Mrksic. So there was a line of command that went from Martic to Mrksic to the subordinates. We also say that the parallel chain of command went from Perisic to Mrksic who was a member of the 40th Personnel Centre. The evidence shows the following, Your Honour: As I mentioned, Martic was the RSK supreme commander. Immediately, immediately before Mrksic became chief of the SVK Main Staff, he was a VJ officer, that is, he was the assistant chief of the VJ General Staff for the land army. He assumed his duty in -- as SVK commander on the 17th of May, 1995 pursuant to a decision in the SVK. If we could go into closed session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session. I assume you want private session actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've seen some of these documents. They are commands. If we could go to P2412. Your Honour, this is the command that we saw earlier today. A command issued by General Perisic to Slobodan Peric and let me just pull it up. So this is corroboration, Your Honour, that General Perisic was issuing commands to personnel in the SVK. This is the 20th of June, 1995, about five weeks after Mrksic had become commander of the SVK. If we go to P177, Your Honour, we have seen this document also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the record, I see on the monitor here it's P1777, not double 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I said double 7, I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said 177.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I seem to recall I made that mistake as well in the trial. Sorry, 1777, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I still see that -- thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can see, Your Honour, this is an order, a naredba, that was issued on the 16th of September, 1995, to General Mrksic who was the commander of the SVK and had been the commander of the SVK since the 17th of May, 1995. Additional corroboration, Your Honour, is found in P1925, which is interesting because this is a command that was issued to the SVK before General Mrksic became commander of the SVK. It was issued on the 24th of March, 1995. Now, finally, if we could turn to Prosecution Exhibit 1340, this is an intercepted communication between Slobodan Milosevic and General Perisic. The relevant text for this part of the submissions, Your Honour, if we could have that up, is Slobodan Milosevic, is making a request to Perisic. "Request contact with Mrksic only and he should not take any orders from Martic." General Perisic's response is quite revealing: "He hasn't been taking any for a long time." Finally, Your Honours, to corroborate the testimony we've been talking about, there is Mr. Borovic's evidence. Mr. Borovic was a Defence witness who was Chef de Cabinet of the VJ General Staff, who testified that General Perisic toured the units of the SVK 11th Corps in the fall of 1995. That testimony is found at 14092. Now, it's our submission, Your Honour, that the principle of unity of command is not a bar to General Perisic having effective control over the personnel centre members. The facts of the case, in our submission, demonstrate that General Perisic did have effective control over VJ members serving in the personnel centres. He had the material ability to prevent them from committing crimes and punishing them. It was concurrent with the material ability of the commanders of the VRS or the SVK. Now, let me just add, Your Honours, the failure of the VRS and the SVK to exercise their material ability to punish the perpetrators of crimes of VJ members who committed crimes in Croatia and in Bosnia does not relieve General Perisic of his responsibility to punish his subordinates. Otherwise you'd have a gross loop-hole in the law. A commander could send his troops into a different state. They could commit crimes. The receiving state would not punish them, and is that an excuse for General Perisic or the commander who has effective control from the sending state to do nothing? It's our submission it is not. In fact, it would undercut the protective measures offered by international law. General Perisic was obliged, Your Honour, to take action against his subordinates, if he knew they had committed crimes while they were serving in Croatia and in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hence my question yesterday about re-subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, ask me your question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking it again, but I just say hence my question yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me find your question from yesterday because I have my transcript here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if you want to address it, the question was simply whether by going over to the other army, is this not a re- subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I do recall, Your Honour, we had the discussion on the terms because there's re-subordination, there's subordination, and we didn't want to get hung up by the lexicon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Subordination is where you, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are saying that these people, as I said, Your Honour, were VJ personnel serving in Bosnia and in Croatia, and as such, Perisic had effective control over them and had the responsibility to deal with their disciplinary measures. Notwithstanding the fact that operational control may have been in the situation of the armies for awhile. The operational control may have existed in the VRS and the SVK. So we say, yes, he did have a responsibility, notwithstanding the whatever we call it, the transfer, the service in those countries. That concludes, Your Honour, my remarks in respect of 7(3). I have some remarks in respect of sentencing. If you'd like me to make them now, I'll happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are in control, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'd be happy to do it. Your Honour, we have briefed the sentencing considerations in our brief. I said we weren't going to repeat the brief in its entirety, but I want to touch on some points. The primary consideration in sentencing and in determining a sentence is the gravity of the crime. Making that assessment, there are two elements that the Court has to consider. The seriousness of the underlying crimes, and the form and degree of participation of General Perisic. Now, the seriousness of the underlying crimes, the Sarajevo cases have been litigated twice; the Zagreb missile attack has been litigated before this institution; Srebrenica has been litigated four or five times before this institution; courts in this institution have found those crimes to be serious. I don't intend to expand or make any additional comments on the seriousness of those crimes, Your Honour. Decisions in this court have spoken for themselves. The facts speak for themselves. I'd like to turn to the form and the degree of participation of the accused, which in this case, Your Honour, is somewhat detached, if you will. General Perisic never fired a bullet, he never personally killed anyone, he never personally set fire to a house in Bosnia or in Croatia, he never personally drove a non-Serb from his home. The conduct which he participated is criminal conduct by virtue of those facts may seem less repugnant to us, much less repugnant to our sensibilities, I understand is most always the case. We have a reaction to people who we see who are the hand-on killers, the people who have blood on their hands. The people who terrorise people, force them to leave from their homes, destroy their cultural sites and their monuments. Physical distance, however, Your Honour, from the actual crimes or lack of a hands-on involvement of those crimes is certainly less jarring, it's natural to our sensibilities. General Perisic is charged with aiding and abetting the people who did all of those things, who killed people, who forcibly displaced people, who ran a sniping and shelling campaign. In our submission, Your Honour, given the protracted nature of the crimes and the magnitude of the crimes, that form of participation should not lessen his responsibility. His assistance to the VRS endured throughout his tenure as Chief of the General Staff, and it was during that period of time some of the most significant crimes occurred. Now, another consideration, and I touched on it earlier, that Your Honours should consider is that General Perisic harboured General Mladic. General Mladic is one of the only two remaining indictees who has not been arrested. We submit, Your Honour, that those acts are relevant to your consideration when deciding what sentence to impose. Now, the Defence brief sets forth a number of mitigating factors. Let me just say his co-operation with the Office of the Prosecutor, he did agree to sit down and have a meeting with the Prosecutor. There was a succession of interviews with us. However, General Perisic was not entirely forthright and it's our submission that that co-operation should attract no weight in mitigation. General Perisic voluntarily surrendered. The Tribunal has given consideration to that, I'm fully aware of that. It's our submission, however, that measured against the magnitude of the crimes that we are considering in this case, that voluntary surrender should also attract little weight. Now, we heard through the trial a number of witnesses who testified about General Perisic's opposition to Slobodan Milosevic. Let's be perfectly clear: During the period through the war, General Perisic was not in opposition to Slobodan Milosevic. The two of them were two of the most important people in the assistance that was given to the VRS and the SVK. Moreover, the opposition to Slobodan Milosevic, which is at the end of his tenure, and we heard testimony about the Kosovo war, General Perisic was not opposed to using the army in Kosovo had there been a declaration of war, but there wasn't, and under those circumstances, he was opposed. He wasn't opposed to the war, however. It's our submission, Your Honour, that his opposition to Milosevic at the end of his tenure should have no weight in terms of mitigating a sentence for these enormous crimes. Your Honour, it is our request that Your Honours convict General Perisic on all counts in the indictment and that you impose a sentence of life for the commission of those crimes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith will be the first to address the Court. That is how we have divided our -- just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We are just doing a quick podium transfer, Your Honour, then I'll be ready to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith, except that there is an echo that I'm hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So am I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not coming through here because I hear it even when I remove the earphone. I don't know what noise that is. You may proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Initially, I would like to echo the thanks that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not a problem, not a problem at all. Initially I would like to echo the thanks that was given by Mr. Harmon to all of the participants who work at this institution, who have worked with us during this trial. Some of you we know by name, many of you we know by face, all of you have been invaluable to these proceedings.
